L12@P0: ABSTRACT
L13@P0: In this paper, a novel adaptive quality-based multi-fidelity (AQBMF) surrogate framework is introduced to
L14@P0: maximize the utilization of low-fidelity (LF) data from various domains. The main goal of the proposed method is
L15@P0: to adaptively select and combine LF data, by assessing its quality, to create the most accurate surrogate. The core
L16@P0: idea lies in interpreting the quality levels of LF data sources as the relative importance of LF surrogates that serve
L17@P0: as basis functions in a multi-fidelity (MF) surrogate. Based on this approach, the proposed AQBMF surrogate
L18@P0: framework comprises four main stages. In the first stage, a newly defined augmented MF formulation is constructed, initially assuming equal importance for all LF data sources. In the second stage, LF surrogates are
L19@P0: ranked by importance through the proposed MF basis screening method. In the third stage, promising candidate
L20@P0: surrogates are systematically constructed based on the importance ranking of the LF surrogates. During this
L21@P0: stage, both the selection and filtering of LF data, as well as the hierarchical and ensemble combination-based MF
L22@P0: methods are considered. In the last stage, the best surrogate is selected from the candidates using the proposed
L23@P0: algorithm. Various benchmark test results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed framework.
L24@P0: Finally, engineering application results show that the proposed AQBMF surrogate achieves higher accuracy than
L25@P0: existing ones within the same computational budget.
L26@P0: 1. Introduction
L27@P0: A surrogate model is a data-driven mathematical model that approximates the response of a real-world physical system [1]. Once
L28@P0: constructed, the surrogate models can quickly predict responses, making
L29@P0: them highly effective for processes such as optimization [2–6], uncertainty propagation [7,8], and sensitivity analysis [9], which are often
L30@P0: resource- and time-intensive. Despite these advantages, obtaining sufficient data remains a significant challenge when the behavior of the
L31@P0: physical system is highly complex or its responses are costly to obtain.
L32@P0: To alleviate this problem, the multi-fidelity (MF) surrogate method
L33@P0: emerges as a promising strategy, aggregating auxiliary data from diverse
L34@P0: sources of varying accuracy levels to make accurate predictions [10,11].
L35@P0: The MF surrogate model is a data fusion technique that uses a large
L36@P0: number of inexpensive, less accurate low-fidelity (LF) samples to quickly
L37@P0: capture overall trends and corrects them with a small number of costly,
L38@P0: high-accuracy high-fidelity (HF) samples [10,11]. Due to their characteristic of complementarily leveraging data with different fidelity levels
L39@P0: to create synergy, MF strategies successfully deliver rapid and accurate
L40@P0: solutions to complex real-world problems [12–18].
L41@P0: In real-world scenarios, it is common to encounter MF datasets
L42@P0: containing LF data from multiple sources. Depending on whether the
L43@P0: fidelity levels of multiple LF data sources are known in advance as prior
L44@P0: information, MF surrogates can be broadly classified into (1) hierarchical and (2) ensemble combination approaches. The former method,
L45@P0: especially in early studies, assumes that the fidelity levels are known in
L46@P0: advance, so all LF resources are combined in a hierarchical manner and
L47@P0: then HF data is utilized for calibration. Representative surrogates are
L48@P0: scaling function-based methods [19], Co-Kriging [11], hierarchical
L49@P0: Kriging (HK) [20], improved hierarchical Kriging (IHK) [21], generalized hierarchical Co-Kriging (GCK) [22], MF surrogate based on design
L50@P0: variable correlations (MFS-DVC) [23], and ensemble learning based MF

L62@P1: not known in advance, applying hierarchical combination methods becomes impossible, prompting more recent studies to address this issue.
L63@P1: In such cases, as in the latter approach, all LF resources are combined in
L64@P1: an ensemble manner, while HF data is utilized for correction. Methods
L65@P1: like linear regression MF surrogate (LR-MFS) [25], extended Co-Kriging
L66@P1: (ECK) [26], variance-weighted sum MF surrogate (VWS-MFS) [27], nonhierarchical Co-Kriging (NHLF-Co-Kriging) [28], extended hierarchical
L67@P1: Kriging (EHK) [29], local correlation-weighted fusion-based MF surrogate (LCWF-MFS) [30], and weighted-sum of multi-HK (WSMHK) [31]
L68@P1: fall under this approach. However, in practice, differences in fidelity
L69@P1: levels may exist among LF sources, even if they are not explicitly labeled.
L70@P1: This suggests that in certain situations, hierarchical MF models may
L71@P1: offer advantages over ensemble-based ones. In particular, the definition
L72@P1: of non-hierarchical relationships is often ambiguous in industrial settings. For instance, suppose there are two LF sources, and the first has a
L73@P1: slightly higher correlation with the HF data than the second. In such a
L74@P1: case, it is unclear whether the two LF sources should be treated in a
L75@P1: hierarchical or ensemble manner. This ambiguity makes it difficult to
L76@P1: determine which type of MF modeling—hierarchical or ensemble—is
L77@P1: more appropriate. Moreover, there are cases where both LF sources have
L78@P1: weak correlations with the HF data individually. Yet, when combined in
L79@P1: a hierarchical manner, their joint information may result in a much
L80@P1: stronger correlation. Although such scenarios are realistic, existing
L81@P1: ensemble-based MF methods have not considered them. In other words,
L82@P1: when fidelity information is unavailable, existing methods do not provide guidance on which approach—hierarchical or ensemble—is more
L83@P1: reasonable.
L84@P1: Besides, existing MF methods have another critical limitation that
L85@P1: they unconditionally use all LF data sources without scrutiny. Contrary
L86@P1: to the common assumption in many MF studies that LF data is always
L87@P1: informative, in practice, low-quality LF data can negatively impact the
L88@P1: MF surrogate model. For example, if the quality of LF data is poor, it can
L89@P1: be detrimental to identifying the overall trend when constructing an MF
L90@P1: surrogate. Moreover, even if high-quality LF data is available, a lack of
L91@P1: sufficient LF data can hinder the construction of an accurate MF surrogate. For example, LF data may be of good quality but generated long
L92@P1: ago, making it impossible to reproduce, thereby hindering trend identification due to insufficient LF data when constructing an MF surrogate.
L93@P1: These situations are frequently encountered in industrial environments.
L94@P1: In the worst-case scenario, the accuracy of the MF surrogate may fall
L95@P1: below that of a single-fidelity (SF) surrogate constructed solely with HF
L96@P1: samples. Therefore, careful consideration is required when applying the
L97@P1: MF method. Existing studies have utilized discriminant metrics such as
L98@P1: normalized cross validation error (NCVE) [32], maximum likelihood
L99@P1: estimation (MLE) [32], Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) [19,33]. In
L100@P1: addition, attempts have been made to address this issue by excluding
L101@P1: only highly biased LF data sources when building the MF surrogates
L102@P1: [34]. However, these studies still have the limitation that they only
L103@P1: consider the effect of a single LF data source among multiple LF data
L104@P1: sources to determine whether to use that LF source. In particular, even if
L105@P1: individual LF sources do not contribute much to the MF surrogate, using
L106@P1: them together can sometimes produce a synergistic effect, which has not
L107@P1: been fully considered in existing research. In other words, existing
L108@P1: studies have not considered the potential coupling effects of multiple LF
L109@P1: sources while determining whether to utilize them.
L110@P1: From the review of existing literature surveys, two ongoing challenges stand out when dealing with multiple LF data sources whose fidelity levels are not pre-defined. Firstly, there is no research on choosing
L111@P1: the appropriate MF combination method. Specifically, there is a need for
L112@P1: studies focusing on choosing between hierarchical and ensemble
L113@P1: combination-based MF methods. Secondly, there is a lack of research on
L114@P1: MF methods that consider the quality of the LF data sources. This involves identifying combinations of LF data sources that produce synergistic effects and pinpointing LF data sources to disregard or overlook.
L115@P1: To the authors’ best knowledge, existing approaches have not effectively
L116@P1: addressed both of these two challenges related to the flexible utilization
L117@P1: of LF data.
L118@P1: In this paper, a novel adaptive quality-based multi-fidelity (AQBMF)
L119@P1: surrogate framework is proposed. This framework introduces a higherlevel decision-making paradigm for the flexible and effective utilization of multiple LF data sources. The key innovation of this study lies in
L120@P1: proposing a unified and adaptive framework that constructs the best
L121@P1: surrogate model for a given scenario. Unlike conventional approaches
L122@P1: that focus on improving specific surrogate formulations, the proposed
L123@P1: method guides the selection and application of surrogate strategies—such as hierarchical-based, quality-aware ensemble-based, or
L124@P1: even SF models—based on the characteristics and quality of the available data. To systematically orchestrate multiple data sources, the core
L125@P1: idea involves treating the quality levels of LF data sources as the relative
L126@P1: significance of the LF surrogates, which serve as basis functions, also
L127@P1: known as trend functions, for the MF surrogate. Based on this idea, the
L128@P1: proposed AQBMF method consists of four main stages: (1) construction
L129@P1: of an augmented MF formulation, (2) MF basis screening, (3) candidate
L130@P1: surrogate generation, and (4) best surrogate selection. The effectiveness
L131@P1: of the proposed method is demonstrated through various numerical and
L132@P1: engineering examples.
L133@P1: The main contributions of the proposed method can be summarized
L134@P1: as follows:
L135@P1: • A novel AQBMF surrogate method is introduced, providing a higherlevel paradigm for adaptive selection and combination of LF sources,
L136@P1: particularly when prior fidelity information is unavailable.
L137@P1: • The proposed framework systematically incorporates multiple LF
L138@P1: sources through a four-stage procedure, by treating LF data quality as
L139@P1: the relative importance (ranking) of basis functions in the MF
L140@P1: surrogate.
L141@P1: • The proposed method achieves superior performance compared to
L142@P1: existing approaches under limited computational budgets through
L143@P1: systematic surrogate model generation.
L144@P1: The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 provides a comprehensive review of conventional MF surrogates and basis
L145@P1: screening methods. Section 3 provides a step-by-step explanation of the
L146@P1: newly proposed AQBMF surrogate framework. In Section 4, the superiority of the proposed method is validated through various numerical
L147@P1: examples. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines potential
L148@P1: avenues for future research.

L197@P2: 2.2. Basis selection method
L198@P2: This section explains the method for selecting basis functions when
L199@P2: constructing surrogate models. In general, selecting appropriate basis
L200@P2: functions has a significant impact on improving the performance of the
L201@P2: surrogate model. As mentioned earlier in Section 2.1, in the Kriging
L202@P2: method, a response typically comprises two main components, the mean
L203@P2: structure and the stochastic parts. In ordinary Kriging, the mean structure is assumed to be constant, while in universal Kriging, it is typically
L204@P2: constructed as a first- or second-order polynomial function. Therefore,
L205@P2: the choice of basis functions in the mean structure part plays a critical
L206@P2: role in determining the performance of Kriging. Several research studies
L207@P2: have explored different approaches for selecting these basis functions,
L208@P2: such as blind Kriging [38], dynamic Kriging [39], and basis screening
L209@P2: Kriging [40]. Among them, the basis screening Kriging method [40] is
L210@P2: known for being more accurate and efficient than other approaches. The
L211@P2: algorithm for this technique can be summarized as follows:
L212@P2: Step 1: Set a maximum order for polynomial basis functions.
L213@P2: Step 2: Estimate the significance of individual basis functions.
L214@P2: Step 3: Gradually add the basis functions based on their estimated
L215@P2: importance, constructing the candidate basis function set.
L216@P2: Step 4: Identify the optimal basis function set from the candidate set
L217@P2: using cross-validation error.
L218@P2: 3. Proposed AQBMF surrogate framework
L219@P2: In this section, a novel AQBMF surrogate framework that fully leverages LF data is proposed. Firstly, the approach to reinterpreting the
L220@P2: MF surrogate model from the perspective of basis functions is introduced. Secondly, the proposed MF framework is illustrated step-by-step.
L221@P2: Sequentially, a validation metric and the overall procedure of the proposed method are described.
L222@P2: 3.1. Thoughts on the MF surrogate
L223@P2: This section elaborates on our insights into the MF surrogate model.
L224@P2: In real-world industrial settings, it is common to encounter a lack of HF
L225@P2: data required to develop predictive models in the current domain, as
L226@P2: shown in Fig. 1. In such cases, leveraging low-cost LF data from various
L227@P2: domains to construct data fusion models, such as MF surrogates, can be a
L228@P2: promising solution. Many previous studies have successfully applied MF
L229@P2: surrogates with the support of high-quality LF data that effectively
L230@P2: reflect the underlying physics. However, it cannot be guaranteed that
L231@P2: such LF information will always be beneficial for HF data. In the worst
L232@P2: scenario, poor-quality LF data can even degrade the overall surrogate
L233@P2: performance. Moreover, it can be challenging even for physics domain
L234@P2: experts to distinguish the quality levels of LF data sources. Therefore, it
L235@P2: is essential to develop data-driven methods that automatically determine how to effectively utilize multiple LF data sources.
L236@P2: To address these challenges, in this study, we focus on the formulation of Kriging and HK in terms of basis functions in surrogate models.
L237@P2: As mentioned earlier in Section 2.1, both data-driven models are divided
L238@P2: into a mean structure part and a stochastic part, where the mean
L239@P2: structure takes the form of a multiplication of the basis function set and
L240@P2: the coefficient vector. Afterwards, the estimated hyper-parameters
L241@P2: through MLE depend on how the basis function set is configured,
L242@P2: naturally influencing the values of the coefficient vector and other
L243@P2: components. Here, when the polynomial function set is employed as
L244@P2: basis functions, it becomes a Kriging model. On the other hand, utilizing
L245@P2: an LF data-driven surrogate that efficiently captures the system’s trend
L246@P2: as basis functions results in an HK model. Therefore, MF surrogate
L247@P2: modeling can be redefined as an efficient surrogate modeling approach
L248@P2: that utilizes high-quality basis vectors. In other words, Kriging is a
L249@P2: special case of HK where the basis function is a polynomial function.
L250@P2: Based on these insights, the use of multiple LF data sources can be
L251@P2: addressed by translating from a physical perspective to a surrogate
L252@P2: model perspective. Generally, LF data contribute to the construction of
L253@P2: an MF surrogate in the form of LF surrogates. Moreover, the performance of these LF surrogates directly impacts the performance of the MF
L254@P2: surrogate as basis functions. Therefore, this study interprets the quality
L255@P2: levels of LF data sources as the relative importance of basis functions
L256@P2: within the MF surrogate, which can be summarized as follows:
L257@P2: • High-quality LF sources can be considered important basis functions
L258@P2: in the surrogate model.
L259@P2: • Low-quality LF sources can be regarded as less important basis
L260@P2: functions in the surrogate model.
L261@P2: Here, when MF surrogates such as scaling function-based methods (e.
L262@P2: g., the comprehensive approach [19]) are used instead of the HK model
L263@P2: mainly employed in this study, the importance of the basis function can
L264@P2: be interpreted as the importance of the trend function.
L265@P2: To better understand the proposed insights, Fig. 2 illustrates surrogate models using various LF data sources. Fig. 2 clearly shows that the
L266@P2: performance of surrogate models can vary, even with the same set of HF
L267@P2: samples, depending on the quality of LF data sources (i.e., basis vectors).

L292@P3: 3.2. Main concept of the proposed method
L293@P3: The main concept of the proposed AQBMF method is to maximize the
L294@P3: performance of the surrogate by appropriately utilizing multiple LF data
L295@P3: sources, whose fidelity levels are not known in advance. This study is
L296@P3: based on the insights from Section 3.1, which interprets the quality
L297@P3: levels of LF data sources as the relative importance of basis functions in
L298@P3: the MF surrogate model. The proposed AQBMF surrogate framework
L299@P3: consists of four main stages. In the first stage, the proposed augmented
L300@P3: MF surrogate formulation is constructed by integrating all available LF
L301@P3: information. The second stage involves estimating the importance of LF
L302@P3: surrogates using the proposed MF basis screening method. In the third
L303@P3: stage, based on the relative importance of LF surrogates, promising
L304@P3: candidate surrogates are systematically generated. Finally, in the fourth
L305@P3: stage, the proposed surrogate selection algorithm chooses the best surrogate from the candidates. The detailed strategies for each stage will be
L306@P3: explained in the following sections. Additionally, it should be noted that
L307@P3: the term ensemble method in this study refers to weight-based ensemble
L308@P3: combination in Eq. (3), rather than ensemble learning, which involves
L309@P3: combining different types of surrogate models.
